hints: Look carefully at the arrow labelled direction of transport. Which side is loading sucrose into the sieve tube (cell Y end) and which side is unloading it (cell Z end)?
Remember that phloem translocation is from source to sink, but a source leaf can feed sinks both above it (like buds and fruits) and below it (like roots). Also recall which sugar is actually loaded.
walkthrough:
**Spot the source and the sink**

Look at the diagram side by side with the arrow. Cell Y is next to the companion cell on the left where flow starts, so this is where loading happens. Cell Z is on the right where flow arrives after a long distance, so this is where unloading happens.

Rule to remember: source loads, sink unloads.

**Use translocation direction**

Translocation in phloem is from source to sink, but it is not only upwards like xylem water. It can go up or down depending on where the sink is.

A photosynthetic leaf (source) can send sucrose up to a growing shoot or fruit, or down to a root for respiration or storage.

**Check the sugar and the tissue**

Phloem loads and transports sucrose, not glucose. Glucose is too reactive. The source (cell Y end) is normally in photosynthetic tissue, while the sink (cell Z end) is normally in non-photosynthetic tissue that needs sugar, like a root, fruit or growing point.

options.A: Cell Y is at the loading end where transport starts, so it is the source cell, not the sink cell.
options.B: Cell Z is the sink receiving sucrose. A sink can be above the source (e.g. fruit, bud) or below the source (e.g. root), so translocation can be up or down.
options.C: Cell Z is the sink where unloading occurs, so it is typically in non-photosynthetic tissue that uses or stores sugar, not photosynthetic tissue.
options.D: Loading into the sieve tube via the companion cell uses sucrose, the transport sugar of phloem, not glucose.
